clue.text: Resort in the USA, or make Persian go elsewhere?

indicators.note: read it as re-sort, with the stress on the second half, and it asks for a fresh ordering rather than a holiday

parts.note: ten letters, and not one of them stays where the clue put it

explanation.walkthrough: Half the clues in this grid open with 'Resort in' somewhere abroad; here the word is not naming a town at all but telling you to sort the letters again. A Persian is a cat, and 'go' is the polite verb.
explanation.definitionFit: make Persian go elsewhere? -> HOUSE-TRAIN: a Persian is a cat, and house-training one teaches it to relieve itself in the tray rather than the carpet.

clue.text: Slick cat almost rampant?

indicators.note: almost there means you stop just before the end, so the final letter never gets written
in heraldry a beast rampant is reared up on its hind legs, and this creature stands its letters on end too

parts.note: the cat is a LION and 'almost' stops one short of its N

explanation.walkthrough: Heraldry is where the surface and the wordplay part company: a rampant lion is a picture, and a rampant three letters is an instruction to read them the other way.
explanation.definitionFit: Slick -> OIL: a slick on the sea is a floating film of crude, so the word names the substance by the shape it makes on water.

clue.text: Bones in line while erect

indicators.note: something erect has been stood upright, and in a down entry upright means reading from the bottom square towards the top

parts.note: an arc is a line, the curved kind a compass draws
as in 'he whistled while he worked' — while and as both mean during the time that

explanation.walkthrough: Anatomy keeps its Latin plurals, which is how a definition with no S on it can still be asking for more than one bone.
explanation.definitionFit: Bones -> SACRA: the sacrum is the wedge of fused vertebrae at the base of the spine, and sacra is its Latin plural.

clue.text: As good as knight, ultimately, soldier on a horse

indicators.note: in a down entry one thing sits on another by standing above it, so this piece goes in first
ultimately means in the end, so only the very end of the word beside it is wanted

parts.note: the very end of KNIGHT, which is what 'ultimately' asks for
soldier ants are the big-jawed caste of a colony, and a bare 'soldier' is the crossword's usual way of asking for one
the article is taken at face value
a rider's mount is the horse being ridden

explanation.walkthrough: Four military-looking words in a row and the definition is the quiet phrase at the front, which is where a clue this cavalry-minded least wants you to look.
explanation.definitionFit: As good as -> TANTAMOUNT: tantamount means amounting to the same thing, so a silence tantamount to a refusal is a silence as good as one.

clue.text: Sharp pilot with habitual mannerism

parts.note: an ace is a pilot with a tally of kills, a usage that dates from the First World War
a tic is the twitch or catchphrase someone repeats without meaning to

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a taste, not an edge — which is the whole misdirection, since 'Sharp' opening a clue reads as a knife or a mind.
explanation.definitionFit: Sharp -> ACETIC: acetic acid is what makes vinegar vinegar, so acetic describes the mouth-puckering sourness we call a sharp taste.

clue.text: Resort in France worth a visit?

definitions.meaning: the Cote d'Azur town at the end of the Promenade des Anglais
somewhere worth going to is a pleasant place, and the everyday adjective for that is the same word

explanation.walkthrough: Punk's running gag in this grid is 'Resort in' as a signal to shuffle letters; this is the one time it means exactly what it says, and the joke is that nothing happens to it at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses at once: the Riviera town on the Baie des Anges, and the everyday adjective for something pleasant enough to be worth going to see.

clue.text: Traveller in Indian state picked up?

indicators.note: a sound you pick up is one you catch by ear, so the state is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: Goa is the small state on India's west coast, and a British speaker says it GO-uh, which is also how an unstressed -er ending comes out

explanation.walkthrough: Non-rhotic English is the whole trick: the r at the end is written but not sounded, so a place in India and a word for a wanderer arrive at the same noise.
explanation.definitionFit: Traveller -> GOER: a goer is anything that goes — a horse, a car, a party guest — naming a traveller by the going rather than the journey.

clue.text: Killer sandwiches in syrup

indicators.note: to sandwich something is to press it between two layers, so one word closes around the other

parts.note: a grenade is thrown to kill, and it splits open one letter from the end
the little word goes in whole, exactly as it is written

explanation.walkthrough: Grenade and grenadine share a root: both come from the pomegranate, the weapon for its shape and its scatter of seed-like fragments.
explanation.definitionFit: syrup -> GRENADINE: the deep red pomegranate syrup poured into a tequila sunrise, sweet and alcohol-free despite the cocktail company it keeps.

clue.text: Adapted like frogs, say, in cold temperature: different in shivering mice

indicators.note: a shiver is what a body does when it cannot hold still, and letters that cannot hold still end up somewhere else
what is in something sits inside it, so this piece is planted among the letters rather than added to the end

parts.note: C is the letter on the cold tap, and the standard abbreviation for it
T for temperature, as on a weather chart or in a physics formula
the rodents' four letters join the two abbreviations to make the six that get shuffled
a different one is another one — the other one

explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' is the flag that frogs are only an example: plenty of other creatures are built the same way, and the answer is the class word covering all of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Adapted like frogs, say -> ECTOTHERMIC: an ectotherm draws its heat from outside its body, which is the technical name for what everyone else calls cold-blooded.

clue.text: City in Spain with the greatest specialised language: English

parts.note: Muhammad Ali called himself The Greatest and the title stuck to him
cant is the private jargon of a trade or a sect, thieves' cant being the best known
E is the usual one-letter stand-in for English

explanation.walkthrough: The colon does no work at all. It only lets 'specialised language: English' read as one idea, when the two halves are separate pieces of the build.
explanation.definitionFit: City in Spain -> ALICANTE: the port on the Costa Blanca, capital of its own province and one of the largest cities on the Spanish Mediterranean.

clue.text: Island featuring a forge

indicators.note: a film featuring an actor has that actor somewhere inside it, so this letter goes in among the others

parts.note: Crete is the big Greek island, and it opens up in the middle
the article is taken as the single letter it is written with

explanation.walkthrough: A holiday island and a blacksmith make a tidy picture, and the picture is the trap: the verb at the end is the definition, not part of the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: forge -> CREATE: forge in its smithy sense means to hammer something into being, so both words mean to make — not the counterfeiter's forge the surface offers.

clue.text: Italian song I adore you, having renounced love for drink

indicators.note: to renounce something is to give it up, so the letter for love is dropped

parts.note: ti amo is Italian for I love you
love is zero in tennis scoring, which looks like the letter O
an aria is a solo song in Italian opera

explanation.surface: An Italian love song whose singer gives up on romance and turns to drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Having renounced love' takes O from TIAMO, leaving TIAM, which goes before ARIA.
explanation.definitionFit: Tia Maria is a coffee-flavoured liqueur, so it names a drink.

clue.text: Resort in India? Drat! West Indian!

indicators.note: read as re-sort, to sort again, so the letters of the words that follow are sorted into a new order

explanation.surface: A holidaymaker curses a resort in India, mistaking it for a Caribbean one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resort' looks like a holiday spot, as in other clues of this puzzle, but it means re-sort: rearrange IN INDIA DRAT, the 'in' included.
explanation.definitionFit: A Trinidadian comes from Trinidad, an island of the West Indies, so is one kind of West Indian.

clue.text: Indian style island welcomes first of tourists

indicators.note: you welcome a guest into your house, so the island takes this letter inside it

parts.note: Bali is the Indonesian island, and it splits after its third letter

indicators.note: of all the letters in the word that follows, only the one at the front is wanted

parts.note: the front letter of TOURISTS

explanation.walkthrough: The geography is a decoy. The island that opens up is Indonesian, several thousand miles from the cuisine the definition is naming.
explanation.definitionFit: Indian style -> BALTI: a balti is a style of curry cooked and served in a pressed-steel bowl, Birmingham's own contribution to Indian cooking.

clue.text: So boy south of Capri perhaps is brother

indicators.note: south is downwards on a map, and in a down entry downwards means further along, so these letters land underneath

parts.note: the Capri was a Ford, and 'perhaps' marks it as one example of a car
thus and so are the same word for in this manner
Ian is the boy the grid wants; crosswords keep a small stable of usable names

explanation.walkthrough: Capri is an island and a Ford at once, which is why 'perhaps' is there — it warns you the word is an example of something rather than the thing itself.
explanation.definitionFit: brother -> CARTHUSIAN: a Carthusian is a monk of the order founded at the Grande Chartreuse, and monks of any order are addressed as Brother.

clue.text: Weaselly words in house

indicators.note: weasel words wriggle out of meaning what they say, and letters that wriggle will not stay in the order they were given

parts.note: seven letters, rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: 'Weaselly words' is a real phrase for evasive language, which is exactly what makes it invisible as an instruction — and 'in' here is fodder, not a container.
explanation.definitionFit: house -> WINDSOR: the surname the British royal family adopted in 1917, and a royal house is a dynasty rather than a building.

clue.text: Resort in Cuba priced on shortage of milk in country

indicators.note: read as re-sort, resort means sort again, so the letters are put into a new order
a shortage means coming up short, so the last letter of milk is lost

parts.note: losing its last letter leaves MIL

explanation.surface: A holiday resort in Cuba where milk is scarce and expensive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resort' looks like a holiday spot, as in the puzzle's other themed clues, but read it as re-sort: the letters of IN CUBA PRICED ON plus MIL ('shortage of' milk) are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dominican Republic is a Caribbean nation sharing the island of Hispaniola with Haiti.

clue.text: Resort in France visited by one part of the set?

definitions.note: The answer is plural and 'part' is singular: the four canines are counted together as a single named part of a full set of teeth.

indicators.note: a visitor ends up inside the place they visit, so this letter goes in among the town's own

parts.note: Cannes is the film-festival resort on the Riviera, and it opens after CAN
one is I, the Roman numeral

explanation.walkthrough: Every other 'Resort in' clue in this grid is a signal to shuffle letters, so the trap here is that this one really is a town. And the set is a mouthful of teeth, not the film set Cannes has just conjured.
explanation.definitionFit: part of the set? -> CANINES: a full set of teeth divides into incisors, canines, premolars and molars, so the canines are one named part of it.

clue.text: Maybe brilliant daughter without domestic staff, running about

indicators.note: running about means going round and back, so the letters are read in reverse order

parts.note: a house without domestic staff has no maid
D is the standard abbreviation for daughter, as in family trees

explanation.surface: A clever daughter has no help at home and dashes around doing everything herself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without domestic staff' is the phrase NO MAID, which 'running about' turns round; 'brilliant' is a noun here, a cut of gem.
explanation.definitionFit: A brilliant is a diamond cut with many facets to maximise sparkle, so it is one example of the gem.

clue.text: Flowers, many on street

indicators.note: to tack one thing on to another is to add it at the end, so these letters follow the ones named next

parts.note: ST is how street is abbreviated on an envelope
reams of it means loads of it; a ream is five hundred sheets of paper

explanation.walkthrough: The comma after the first word is doing honest work: it fences off the definition, and the definition has nothing to do with petals.
explanation.definitionFit: Flowers -> STREAMS: read as flow-ers, things that flow — the crossword staple that turns a garden word into rivers.

clue.text: Nurse touching tissue

parts.note: to nurse a wound is to tend it
two things touching are one on the other, so touching gives ON

explanation.walkthrough: Three medical-sounding words in a row and the surface never leaves the ward, so nothing in it warns you that a charade is being assembled.
explanation.definitionFit: tissue -> TENDON: a tendon is the tough fibrous cord of connective tissue tying muscle to bone, so the definition names what it is made of.

clue.text: State when I should cut hair

indicators.note: to cut into something is to make your way inside it, so this letter lands in the middle of the word that follows

parts.note: a mane is the hair on a horse's or a lion's neck, and it opens after two letters
the pronoun is taken as the single letter it is written with

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a barber's appointment and the answer is on a map. 'Cut' is the pivot: a haircut in one reading, an incision into a word in the other.
explanation.definitionFit: State -> MAINE: the north-easternmost of the United States, so the definition is the general category and the answer one instance of it.

clue.text: See 15
Observed in Marbella, this club

indicators.note: what is observed in a place was already sitting there in plain view, waiting for somebody to notice it

parts.note: the last two letters of the resort run straight on into the first three of THIS

explanation.walkthrough: Marbella is a Spanish resort in a puzzle full of resorts, which is precisely why you read past it — and past 'this', a word that normally points at something rather than spelling it.
explanation.definitionFit: club -> LATHI: a lathi is the long iron-bound bamboo stave carried by Indian police, so 'club' is the plain English word for the thing.

clue.text: Conclusion yet to be reached in a riddle — yeh, right!

indicators.note: a word whose conclusion is not yet reached stops short, so its last letter is missing

parts.note: to riddle is to pass through a sieve, to sift

explanation.surface: Someone scoffing at a riddle whose answer never arrives.
explanation.walkthrough: Riddle means a puzzle on the surface but here is the sieving verb; with its 'Conclusion yet to be reached', SIFT stops at SIF.
explanation.definitionFit: 'As if!' is a sarcastic exclamation of disbelief, much like saying yeah, right.

clue.text: Fishes Charlie gutted eaten by Jimmy?

indicators.note: a gutted fish has had its insides taken out, and so has this word — only the two outer letters survive

parts.note: a Jimmy Riddle is rhyming slang for a piddle, shortened to Jimmy, and it opens up before its last letter

indicators.note: whatever is eaten ends up inside the eater, so those letters sit within the others

parts.note: CHARLIE with its insides removed keeps only its first and last letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'Gutted' meaning emptied of insides is one of the standard signals to keep only a word's outer letters, and a clue about fish makes it almost invisible.
explanation.definitionFit: Fishes -> PISCES: Pisces is the twelfth sign of the zodiac, drawn as a pair of fish, and its English name is simply the Fishes.

clue.text: Resort in Italy paired with Germany in elegant manner

indicators.note: the word splits into re and sort, which is exactly what the letters are being asked to do
to pair one thing with another is to put the two together, so this letter joins the letters being sorted

parts.note: D is Germany's international vehicle code, from Deutschland
seven letters straight off the clue, joining the D in the shuffle

explanation.walkthrough: Three countries in one sentence and only two of them are pulling their weight: Italy for its letters, Germany for its single-letter code, and the resort is not a place at all.
explanation.definitionFit: in elegant manner -> DAINTILY: daintily means with delicate neatness, the way somebody lifts a teacup, so the phrase spells out an adverb of manner.

clue.text: Deity briefly slowing up

indicators.note: said briefly, a word is cut short, so the end of this one is not written
in a down entry up means from the bottom square towards the top, so the letters are read the other way

parts.note: rallentando is the score marking for slowing down, written rall., and briefly that is RAL

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are borrowed vocabulary — a Latin household god and an Italian musical instruction — which is a great deal of Europe for three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Deity -> LAR: a lar was a Roman household god, one of the lares who guarded the hearth and the family that kept its little shrine.

clue.text: Seed spiller with a very tiny part to withdraw?

indicators.note: to withdraw is to draw back the way you came, so the letters are read in the opposite direction

parts.note: nano- is the prefix for a thousand-millionth, the smallest fraction most people ever name

explanation.walkthrough: Nano- reaches English from the Greek for dwarf by way of the SI prefixes, which is a lot of scientific precision to spend on a clue whose definition comes out of Genesis.
explanation.definitionFit: Seed spiller -> ONAN: in Genesis 38 Onan spilled his seed on the ground rather than father a child for his brother, and English took a word from the story.

clue.text: Resort in France is for Zurich gnomes?

indicators.note: read as re-sort, to sort again, so the letters of the words that follow are sorted into a new order

explanation.surface: A holiday resort in France is the destination for Swiss bankers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resort' means re-sort: rearrange IN FRANCE IS, including 'in'. 'Gnomes of Zurich' is a mocking British name for Swiss bankers, coined in the 1960s.
explanation.definitionFit: The gnomes of Zurich is a derisive phrase for Swiss bankers and money men, so they are financiers.
